questions.q: What is the actual relationship between Bicep and ARM templates?
options: ARM templates are being deprecated and no longer work
Bicep and ARM are two completely unrelated deployment systems
Bicep only works for resources that ARM cannot deploy
Bicep is a friendlier authoring syntax that compiles down to ARM template JSON — it never replaced ARM
questions.explain: Every Bicep resource in this chapter is, underneath, an ARM template resource — Bicep is the authoring layer over the same engine.

questions.q: What does `az bicep build` actually produce?
options: The exact ARM template JSON a Bicep file would deploy as anyway — mainly useful for inspection
A deployed Azure resource, without needing az deployment group create
A new .bicep file with optimized syntax
Nothing — the command doesn't exist
questions.explain: Nobody deploys the built JSON directly in normal use; it mainly exists to inspect what a Bicep file compiles to.

questions.q: Why does `az bicep decompile` matter more in practice than `az bicep build`, according to this lesson?
options: Decompile is actually used less often than build in real teams
It lets a team with existing raw ARM templates (or an exported Portal template) start authoring the same infrastructure in Bicep without hand-translating hundreds of lines of JSON
Decompile deploys resources directly, unlike build
There is no practical difference between the two commands
questions.explain: Converting existing ARM JSON into Bicep saves a huge amount of manual translation work for teams migrating to the friendlier syntax.

questions.q: According to this lesson, where does raw ARM JSON still show up today?
options: Only when a deployment fails
Only in Terraform state files
Portal template exports, some older tooling that only accepts ARM JSON, and occasionally a newer resource type where Bicep/Terraform provider support hasn't caught up yet
It never shows up anywhere anymore
questions.explain: Lesson 9's honest note about Fabric Capacity provisioning is a real example of the third case — a genuinely new resource type where support can lag.

questions.q: What ties together Chapter 3's five lessons, per this lesson's recap?
options: Only Terraform content, with no mention of Bicep
A single case study repeated five different ways
Five completely unrelated topics with no common thread
Bicep syntax and resource blocks, then parameters and early error-catching, then the deploy command and dry run, then a real secured deployment, then the ARM JSON underneath all of it
questions.explain: Each lesson built on the last, ending exactly where this lesson explains what all of it was compiling down to the whole time.
